query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Local lattice distortions induced by the random spatial distribution of elements with differing atomic sizes in high-entropy alloys act as barriers to dislocation motion, thereby governing their enhanced hardness and strength.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase equiatomic high-entropy alloy (e.g., a BCC or FCC HEA) with significant atomic size mismatch among its principal elements.
generation.intervention: Systematically modify the alloy composition to reduce (or, in a separate set, further enhance) the atomic size mismatch while keeping the overall phase and grain structure similar.
generation.conditions: Samples processed under identical thermal and mechanical treatments at room temperature (and potentially elevated temperatures) to isolate the effect of lattice distortion on dislocation mobility during standard yield and hardness testing.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of local lattice distortion (variation in interatomic distances) due to compositional complexity.
generation.mechanism: Variations in atomic radii create regions of local strain that impede the motion of dislocations. A higher degree of lattice distortion increases the energy barrier for dislocation glide, leading to increased yield strength and hardness relative to alloys with lower mismatch.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with a higher degree of atomic size mismatch (and thus more pronounced lattice distortions) will show increased hardness and higher yield strength compared to a baseline HEA with minimized size variance, as evidenced by mechanical tests and microstructural dislocation observations.
generation.baseline: A high-entropy alloy with a similar phase (and grain) structure but designed with elements that have more similar atomic radii, resulting in reduced lattice distortion.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis should hold primarily for single-phase solid solutions where grain size, processing history, and secondary precipitation are controlled. It may not apply when multiphase microstructures (with significant precipitate hardening or other extrinsic strengthening mechanisms) dominate the mechanical response.
generation.uncertainty: While the role of lattice distortion is supported by theoretical reasoning and some experimental trends, the quantitative contribution of dislocation pinning by lattice strain versus other mechanisms (such as precipitation or intermetallic formation) remains to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one set with a high atomic size mismatch (maximized lattice distortion) and another with a minimized size mismatch, ensuring both are processed to yield a similar single-phase microstructure and grain size. Perform identical thermal treatments and then subject both sets to systematic hardness (microindentation) and yield strength (tensile/compression) tests. Additionally, use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to track dislocation motion and quantify obstacles in each sample.
measurements: Yield strength from tensile or compression tests
TEM observations of dislocation density and interaction with distorted lattice regions
X-ray diffraction to confirm phase consistency and measure lattice strain
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with a higher atomic size mismatch (and therefore expected greater lattice distortion) does not consistently exhibit a statistically significant increase in hardness and yield strength relative to the controlled baseline alloy, or if TEM shows no additional hindrance to dislocation motion, then the hypothesis that lattice distortion is the governing mechanism for enhanced strength and hardness in HEAs would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).

Machine-learning interatomic potential

In this section, we discuss the results of the development of the interatomic-potential model used to enable the application of MD simulations of dislocation properties in bcc MoNbTaW. We employ the general framework of machine-learning (ML)-based approaches, which have emerged recently as a systematic framework to develop potentials with accuracies near that of the underlying DFT calculations for elemental and multicomponent systems [24] , [44] – [46] . Here, using training data reported previously [24] for elemental, binary, ternary, and quaternary systems in Nb–Ta–Mo–W, we developed a potential for the MoNbTaW RHEA based on the moment tensor potential (MTP) formalism, which has been found to feature an excellent balance between accuracy and computational cost [46] . The flowchart for constructing the MTP is shown in Fig. 1a with the methodological details provided in “Methods”. The basic materials property predictions of the MTP model are provided in Supplementary Table 1 .
